props.title: Prêt-à-Porter

sections.content: Robert Altman's **Prêt-à-Porter** (1994) - also released as "Ready to Wear" - brings his signature overlapping dialogue and sprawling ensemble cast to the cutthroat world of Parisian fashion. Like his masterpiece **Nashville** (1975), Altman weaves multiple storylines through a high-stakes industry event. The film savagely satirizes fashion media, with Julia Roberts and Tim Robbins playing journalists who never leave their hotel room, while Sophia Loren and Marcello Mastroianni bring Old World glamour to this send-up of modern fashion's excesses. The film culminates in a controversial nude runway show that strips away (literally) the industry's pretensions.

sections.content: Fashion documentaries offer fascinating real-world counterpoints to Altman's satire. **The September Issue** (2009) follows Vogue's Anna Wintour with unprecedented access, while **Unzipped** (1995) captures designer Isaac Mizrahi's creative process with intimate detail. These docs reveal the actual chaos and creativity Altman satirizes. More recently, **McQueen** (2018) profiles the tragic genius of Alexander McQueen, showing how the industry's pressures can destroy its brightest talents. SUBHEAD: The Fashion Film Genre Evolution

The intersection of fashion and film reached new heights in the 1990s and 2000s. **Clueless** (1995) turned high school fashion into cultural touchstones, while **Sex and the City** (2008) made Manolo Blahnik a household name. **Funny Face** (1957) established many fashion film tropes with Audrey Hepburn's transformation from bookstore clerk to model. Today's fashion films like **House of Gucci** (2021) focus more on industry drama and true crime elements than pure style celebration.
